contributions.headingText:
Fibroadenoma is a biphasic neoplasm of the terminal duct lobular unit composed of a proliferation of epithelial and stromal elements.

Phyllodes tumour is generally a circumscribed fibroepithelial neoplasm showing a prominent intracanalicular architectural pattern with leaf-like stromal fronds, capped by luminal epithelial and myoepithelial cell layers, accompanied by stromal hypercellularity.

2F30.5 & XH9HE2 Fibroadenoma of breast & Fibroadenoma, NOS

2F30.3 & XH50P7 Benign phyllodes tumour of breast & Phyllodes tumour, benign

2F75 & XH5NK4 Neoplasms of uncertain behaviour of breast & Phyllodes tumour, borderline

2C63 & XH8HJ7 Malignant phyllodes tumour of breast & Phyllodes tumour, malignant
Fibroepithelial tumours may occur in any part of the breast.

Fibroepithelial tumour of the breast often manifests as a palpable mass, with some patients also experiencing pain {32281202; 30628932}. Fibroadenomas can occur synchronously as multiple masses in the same breast or bilaterally {29969836; 31445140; 28299887}. In contrast, phyllodes tumours tend to be unifocal {9422317}. Both can grow to large sizes (> 100 mm) {31991330; 32267738; 30628932}, resulting in breast distortion and asymmetry. There may be thinning of the overlying skin with dilatation and prominence of the superficial veins {5547408}. The breast may feel warm as a result of the increased blood supply, and ischaemia and erosion of the overlying skin may occur in extremely large tumours. Infarction can occur in both tumours and lead to nipple discharge {32061367}.

When assessing breast tumours in the paediatric population, ultrasonography is generally performed because it can detect lesions in dense breast tissue and does not expose paediatric patients to ionizing radiation {30174488}. On ultrasound, both fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumours appear as hypoechoic, oval, solid masses with well-circumscribed margins and posterior acoustic enhancement {20449731; 8539362}. There is considerable overlap of ultrasonographic features, and distinguishing the two on imaging is not always possible {11972459}. Anechoic cysts or clefts may be seen in phyllodes tumour and correspond to the gross appearance of the tumour, but they are not entirely specific because they may also be seen in juvenile fibroadenomas.

Fibroadenoma is the most common breast tumour in adolescent girls {889047; 7118680} and can occur in children as young as 8–9 years old {30476459; 29605260}. In the USA, phyllodes tumours in the paediatric population are reported to be more common in Black children than in White children {31991330; 29605260; 30352693}. Malignant phyllodes tumours are the second most common malignant breast tumours in adolescent girls, after carcinomas {31991330; 28058544; 30352693}.

The exact etiology of fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumour is unclear, because most cases occur sporadically. However, a relationship with estrogenic stimulation has been postulated for fibroadenomas {6092767}. Myxoid fibroadenomas have also been described in women with Carney complex {2069209}. More recently, ciclosporin immunosuppression has been implicated in the development of fibroadenomas in both liver and renal transplant recipients {28556594; 16350824; 9038560}, with resolution of the fibroadenomas observed in some patients upon cessation of ciclosporin immunosuppression {20534252}.

Like adult fibroadenomas, paediatric fibroadenomas also contain MED12 exon 2 mutations in a subset of cases, as seen in two studies {30467240; 29969836}. In addition, in one of the studies, 8 benign phyllodes tumours were sequenced and MED12 mutations were found in 7 tumours {30467240}. A majority of the MED12 exon 2 mutations in benign fibroepithelial tumours were found to be in-frame deletions. MED12 mutations were also associated with the intracanalicular type of growth pattern {30467240}. However, this was not reproduced in the other study, which found MED12 missense mutations in a majority of paediatric fibroepithelial tumours but no correlation between MED12 mutations and type of growth pattern; instead, a correlation was found between MED12 and stromal mitotic counts {29969836}. In both studies, none of the fibroadenomas or benign phyllodes tumours had TERT promoter mutations.

Fibroadenomas are solid, ovoid tumours with a firm, greyish-white cut surface with slit-like spaces. Phyllodes tumours are often larger and show a bulging cut surface with or without cystic spaces. The cut surface can also show a variety of appearances, ranging from firm to soft and fleshy, tan to yellow or greyish, and with gelatinous mucoid areas or papillary excrescences. Haemorrhage and necrosis may be seen in malignant phyllodes tumours {9422317}.

Fibroepithelial tumours show a biphasic proliferation of stromal and epithelial elements. Fibroadenomas classically display a mildly cellular stroma, but in the paediatric population, increased stromal cellularity is not uncommon {25998513} and stromal mitotic counts may even reach 2.5–5 mitoses/mm2 (equating to 5–10 mitoses/10 HPF of 0.5 mm in diameter and 0.2 mm2 in area) in rare cases {28299887}. Small leaf-like fronds may also be present. These features do not necessarily warrant a diagnosis of phyllodes tumour {32267738; 25998513}. Phyllodes tumours in the paediatric age group show similar morphological features to those seen in adults {9422317}. They are characterized by a prominent leaf-like architecture secondary to an exaggerated intracanalicular growth pattern and are associated with a hypercellular stroma. Periductal stromal tumour is regarded as a subtype of phyllodes tumour with a pericanalicular growth pattern. Phyllodes tumour can be divided into benign, borderline, and malignant categories based on the criteria used for adults.

The cytological features of fibroepithelial tumours are similar to those seen in adults. Because paediatric fibroadenomas may have increased stromal cellularity, it may be challenging to distinguish them from phyllodes tumours on cytology.

Fibroadenoma

Essential: a circumscribed biphasic tumour; an intracanalicular and/or pericanalicular growth pattern; no stromal overgrowth; absence of well-developed fronds; no stromal atypia; low mitotic activity in the stromal component.

Phyllodes tumour

Essential: stromal fronds and hypercellularity; a dominant intracanalicular growth pattern with stromal fronds capped by luminal/myoepithelial cell layers.

The majority of fibroadenomas do not recur after excision, even with positive margins {25998513; 28299887}. Phyllodes tumours may recur locally, and malignant phyllodes tumours have the potential to metastasize. Infiltrative tumour borders and positive surgical margins may increase the risk of local recurrence {9422317}. However, a lack of local recurrence has also been reported in some case series of benign phyllodes tumours with positive surgical margins, with clinical follow-up being recommended for phyllodes tumours in the benign category instead of further excision {22507352; 31107366}. Paediatric patients with malignant phyllodes tumours have been found to have better overall survival than older patients {31991330}.
